doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: Chico Hamilton's quote, Broadway jobs and Al Gorgoni
summary: She reflects on musicians losing something in Broadway work, and on Charlie Calello and Al Gorgoni.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: One last thing with this. Chico Hamilton talked about, you know he did this for 15 or 20 years, and he — this is a quote from him. He says, “I started in ’66 until the 80s maybe. I learned how to drink in the daytime, the three martini lunch, and how to schmooze. I made a lot of dough but what good is the dough when you kind of lose something.” So do you know, what is that something that he would have felt?

I certainly know it about guys that went into Broadway. Because Broadway gig was like the bottom of the barrel during that time when there were record dates and so forth. And then when those dates began to go away and people began to take Broadway jobs they lost something and they talked about losing that something. And you know I was fortunate because I was writing most of what I did. I mean I did the first record dates, of course all record dates were wonderful, but I was working with Charlie Calello who did all the Four Seasons stuff you know, and other stuff, and the record dates were well written, were good stuff and fun. And as a rhythm player, I mean Gary Chester was the main one and there were others, and the guitar players changed to the younger guys. Have you heard, do you know Al Gorgoni?

He’s one, he’s a wonderful guitar player, classical as well as, you know. But he was one of the young guys that I met at Associated, and then when I started doing commercials then he was one of the main ones I called you know, because they could get that feel.
